newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW - Swiss open door to hedge funds.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Swiss open door to hedge funds.

text.p: Traditionally conservative Switzerland is actively courting hedge funds, whose aggressive investment tactics have won renown in financial markets for both their fat profits and hefty risks.
In an inderal Banking Commission said that Swiss are opening up to such investments following ground-breaking legal changes.

Romain Marti, deputy director of the Secretariat of the Swiss Federal Banking Commission, believes that the move will benefit both investors and heighten Switzerland's attraction as a financial centre.
He said the Commission was examining applications for Swiss-based "non-traditional" funds and expects at least one such fund, which invests in selected hedge funds, to gain approval soon.
"One is basically free to do a lot" he said.
In the past the Swiss have been limited mainly to old-fashioned investment funds that typically just buy stocks, bonds or money market securities.

But the laws passed in 1995 have given the authorities the scope to start letting in a host of modern alternatives, including the highly leveraged vehicles used by investors liketune from sterling's 1992 collapse and exit from Europe's exchange rate mechanism.

Matthaeus den Otter, a senior officer at the Banking Commission and specialist for non-traditional funds, said the changes were a "paradigm shift" for the country's authorities and would allow investors to take responsibility for themselves.
"One no longer forbids investment funds, but says instead, 'this is a fund which carries a special risk' and provided all risks have been disclosed, then the investors can buy it," den Otter said.

Fund manager ED&F Man Group Plc has already gained approval to sell two 'alternative' investment funds -- the first time ever the Banking Commission gave its approval to such investment vehicles. So far, no domestic funds have been approved in this category.
Marti and den Otter see such non-traditional funds as an ideal way to boost Switzerland's attraction as a financial centre.

In the past the country has faced significant stumbling blocks in its competition with other financial centres like Luxembourg, due to the Swiss penchant to tax certain investment transactions. The country also remains outside the European Union.
This has put "plain vanilla" portfolios at a disadvantage but may actually work in favour of hedge funds.
Switzerland does not levy capital gains taxes, a bonus for returns on non-traditional investments, for example.

Hedge funds also do not fall into the European Union directive on open-ended mutual funds classed as "UCITS" -- Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities -- so hedge funds have no advantage setting up in Luxembourg, or elsewhere in the EU, as opposed to Switzerland.

"We don't want to be a hedge fund regulator, but we want to be open to anyone who wants to be active in this market," Marti said. Den Otter stressed that the Swiss government wants to be open to "serious funds."

Direct marketing of off-shore funds in Switzerland is still prohibited for funds set up in off-shore centres excluded from list of those countries whose supervisory and regulatory systems are recognised by the Swiss.
This includes centres like Bermuda, Bahamas and the Dutch Antilles -- home to many a hedge fund.

But off-shore hedge funds will now be able to market products indirectly through Swiss vehicles as such products will be packaged in such a way that makes them "Swiss." -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
